title: A calculator
description:
Write a calculator that reads one sum per line, like `12.5 * 4`, and prints the answer, until the end of the input:

```
12.5 * 4
7 / 2
10 % 3
2 ^ 10
5 / 0
3 $ 4
hello
```

prints

```
= 50
= 3.5
= 1
= 1024
Cannot divide by zero
Unknown operator: $
Could not read: hello
```

| Operator | Does |
|---|---|
| `+ - * /` | the usual, on doubles |
| `%` | the remainder of the two numbers as whole numbers (both are converted to `long long`); `% 0` is "Cannot divide by zero" |
| `^` | the first number to the power of the second, which is a whole number from 0 to 63 (a loop of multiplications); otherwise `Bad power` |

Print answers with `printf("= %g\n", answer)`: `%g` drops trailing zeros.

Reading a whole line at a time lets you recover from bad input. `fgets` reads one line into a char array (lesson 2.05 explains it), and `sscanf` then reads from that line the way `scanf` reads from the input:

```c
char line[200];
while (fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin) != NULL) {
    double a = 0, b = 0;
    char op = 0;
    if (sscanf(line, "%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b) != 3) { /* could not read */ }
}
```

To print the line in the error message without its new line, use `%.*s` with the length up to the new line, or remove the `'\n'` from the end yourself.
hints: `strcspn(line, "\r\n")` (from `<string.h>`) gives the length up to the first new line, so `line[strcspn(line, "\r\n")] = '\0';` cuts the new line off.

Loops come properly in lesson 2.01, but the starter already shows one: a `while` repeats its body as long as its condition is true. For the power: `double result = 1; int i = 0; while (i < exponent) { result = result * a; i = i + 1; }`.
requirements: Work out the power with a loop of multiplications, not a library function.
stretch: Put the power in its own function, `double power(double base, int exponent)` (functions come in lesson 2.02).
